Question

Are these cases related to each other?

Find out whether cases share a recent common source or belong to the same transmission chain, using whole-genome relatedness.

Genomic relatedness can support or argue against a link between cases, but it cannot prove direct transmission on its own. Combine it with epidemiological information such as dates, locations, and contacts.

Which protocol to use

Choose the group your pathogen belongs to.

If the pathogen is Viruses

  1. Viral phylogenomic surveillance

Look for cases that cluster closely in the phylogeny. During fast spread, unrelated cases can carry identical genomes, so interpret closeness together with collection dates and epidemiological data.

If the pathogen is Bacteria

  1. Bacterial phylogenomic surveillance

Use SNP distances and the phylogeny together, with a cluster threshold appropriate for your species. Filter recombination first so imported regions do not inflate distances.

If the pathogen is Fungi

  1. Fungal phylogenomic surveillance

Use SNP distances and the phylogeny together. Thresholds for linked cases vary widely between fungal species, so use published values for your species where they exist.
